own_scenes.desc: Tras la quema de discos de disco en Comiskey Park y la campaña de la emisora de rock WRIF, el Medio Oeste se volvió hostil al baile, y el disco sobrevivió camuflado en discos de Italia, Francia y Bélgica. Moroder, uno de los primeros dueños de un Moog, convirtió con Pete Bellotte las canciones de baile en epopeyas electrónicas («Love to Love You Baby» de Donna Summer); Cerrone, con «Love in C Minor» (1976), inventó para muchos el «disco conceptual» del que saldrían house y techno. Al levantarse en 1980 las restricciones a la importación, los DJs estadounidenses devoraron el italo-disco: Jacques Fred Petrus (Peter Jacques Band, Macho), Claudio Simonetti de Goblin (Easy Going, Vivian Vee, la banda sonora de College, éxito en el Chicago previo al house), Alexander Robotnick («Problèmes d’Amour», de los primeros discos con la TB-303), Kano («It’s a War», «I’m Ready», «Holly Dolly»), Liaisons Dangereuses («Los Niños del Parque»), Klein & MBO, Telex, Martin Circus. En Detroit se le llamaba «progressive»: chavales negros que no se conformaban con el R&B que se les vendía y escuchaban sobre todo a artistas blancos europeos, un gusto que unió el este y el oeste de la ciudad. El seudónimo múltiple, herencia del italo, sigue siendo la norma en la electrónica.

refs.q: The resulting subgenre, which encompassed a wide spectrum of sounds (including hi-NRG), was summarized as “Eurodisco,” and techno and house owe as much to its electronic upgrade of traditional disco as they do to the rhythms of Kraftwerk.
refs.para: Disco’s continued evolution remained largely hidden from the mainstream, perhaps because the records emanated from unlikely sources such as Italy, France, and Belgium, or simply because the gay community comprised the largest segment of its audience. The resulting subgenre, which encompassed a wide spectrum of sounds (including hi-NRG), was summarized as “Eurodisco,” and techno and house owe as much to its electronic upgrade of traditional disco as they do to the rhythms of Kraftwerk.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Party Out of Bounds: The Pre-History of Techno, 1978–1983

refs.q: In Detroit, Italo-disco would be known simply as “progressive,” which aptly described the generation’s attitude toward music as well.
refs.para: In Detroit, Italo-disco would be known simply as “progressive,” which aptly described the generation’s attitude toward music as well. These African American kids weren’t content to limit themselves to the R&B and “urban contemporary” records being marketed to them; just as much, if not more, of their listening was produced by the mainly white artists of Eurodisco. These records became the most popular music of the high school set, bridging the gap between Detroit’s east and west sides. The electronic sound that was so integral to Eurodisco found a perfect complement in the updated funk and R&B of Shannon (“Let the Music Play”) and of George Clinton’s solo excursions.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Party Out of Bounds: The Pre-History of Techno, 1978–1983

refs.q: “It wasn’t a song,” says Elorious Cain of Ottawa-based ABM Records. “Up until that point there was a tremendous concentration on making songs out of disco.”
refs.para: Parisian Jean-Marc Cerrone was second only to Moroder in terms of stature and influence among Eurodisco’s pioneers. He continued evolving the disco sound after Moroder had moved on to film projects and collaborations with rock artists in the 1980s. Some experts point to Cerrone’s 1976 single “Love in C Minor” as the first recording to sever all ties with traditional musical conventions. “It wasn’t a song,” says Elorious Cain of Ottawa-based ABM Records. “Up until that point there was a tremendous concentration on making songs out of disco.” Cain holds that “Love in C Minor” was the start of “conceptual disco,” from which house, techno, and myriad other styles would flow.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Party Out of Bounds: The Pre-History of Techno, 1978–1983

podcast.title: Early Influence on Belleville Three
podcast.body: Italo Disco was among the European electronic music genres that significantly influenced Juan Atkins, Derrick May, and Kevin Saunderson during their formative years in Belleville. "lo que sería conocido más tarde como Italo Disco."

srcs.episode: Cómo Detroit Reinventó la Música Electrónica ｜ Pioneros del Techno

podcast.title: Initial Focus of Early Megamixes
podcast.body: The second installment of the "Max Mix" series, released six months after the first, was primarily filled with Italo Disco songs and its Spanish counterpart, "Saba de Ishown." This genre was a foundational element for the early Megamix phenomenon in Spain. "un Megamix repleto de canciones de Italo Disco y su versión española, el Saba de Ishown."

srcs.episode: Ritmo y Extorsión: Así Dominaron los Megamix los 90s

podcast.title: Melodic Influence on Eurodance
podcast.body: Italo Disco exerted a strong melodic influence on the nascent Eurodance sound. Its distinctive melodies contributed to the emergence of "more colorful themes" that successfully transitioned from underground clubs to mainstream sales charts. "Además de la fuerte influencia, melodica delital o disco..."

srcs.episode: La gran mentira detrás del Eurodance

podcast.title: Shift in Megamix Sound
podcast.body: After its initial dominance, Italo Disco's presence in Megamixes evolved. The genre gave way to faster and more forceful electronic music styles, such as Acid House, New Beat, EBM, and later Máquina and OroDens, especially after the influence of "La Ruta y el Sonido Valencia." "el fenómeno Megamix empezó a adoptar músicas más rápidas y contundentes que iban más allá delitalo disco."
